notes.meaning: God reminds Jerusalem that she completely forgot where she came from. When she was born, she was like an unwanted baby left to die in the dirt until God rescued and raised her. Forgetting His mercy made her proud and led her straight into worshipping false gods.

The Lord cries out in sorrow and warning over Jerusalem's terrible course of sin. On top of all her earlier sins, the city built pagan shrines and brothels in every public square. She shamelessly paraded her spiritual unfaithfulness where everyone could see it.

Jerusalem built idol altars at every street corner and made herself cheap and disgraceful. Instead of cherishing the beauty God gave her, she offered herself to any foreign god or nation that walked past. She became like an immoral woman actively chasing after strangers.

The people turned to Egypt, trusting in that nation's strength and adopting its filthy religious customs. They relied on Egyptian soldiers instead of depending on the Lord who had saved them out of slavery. This deliberate unfaithfulness stirred up God's righteous anger.

God disciplined Jerusalem by cutting back her land and food, just as a husband might reduce the allowance of an unfaithful wife. He also allowed her enemies, the Philistines, to conquer and humiliate her. Even those pagan neighbors were shocked by how easily Jerusalem tossed aside her own God.

Even after being corrected, Jerusalem refused to turn back to God. Instead, she reached out to the distant Assyrians, making political treaties and adopting their idols. Her craving for false gods was totally out of control and could never be satisfied.

Jerusalem pushed her unfaithfulness even farther by copying Babylon, the wealthy trading empire of the Chaldeans. She welcomed their idols alongside all the Canaanite customs she already practiced. Yet no matter how many foreign gods she chased, her heart was still empty and restless.

God describes Jerusalem's heart as diseased, weak-willed, and lacking all moral strength. At the exact same time, she acted like a stubborn, haughty woman who refused to be told what to do. The strength of a person's wild desires only proves how weak their inner self really is.

Jerusalem built idol shrines at every corner, but she was even worse than a common prostitute. A prostitute sells herself because she wants payment to survive. Jerusalem did not even want payment; she gave herself away freely just for the thrill of sinning.

Jerusalem acted like an unfaithful wife who invites strangers into her bed instead of loving her own husband. She already had a devoted provider in God, who gave her everything she could ever need. Turning her back on Him to chase foreign nations was pure, brazen betrayal.

Men normally pay money to hire a prostitute, but Jerusalem did the complete opposite. She took her own silver, gold, and royal treasures to bribe foreign nations and their gods to come to her. Her spiritual adultery was utterly backwards because she paid her lovers instead of being paid by them.

The Lord addresses Jerusalem by her true spiritual name—a prostitute—and orders her to stand and hear His court verdict. The prophet speaks like a judge reading a formal legal sentence. Because Jerusalem refused to obey God's law of love, she must now listen to His sentence of punishment.

God reads the list of charges against the guilty city before sentencing her. She threw away her wealth on disgusting idols and shamelessly exposed herself in spiritual adultery. Worst of all, she committed murder by sacrificing her own little children in the fire to pagan gods.

God announces that He will gather all the nations Jerusalem allied with, both former friends and old enemies. He will strip the city bare so they can all look at her shame and ruin. The very world powers Jerusalem trusted in to save her will be the ones God uses to humiliate her.

God declares that Jerusalem will be sentenced under the law as an adulteress and a murderer. Because she slaughtered innocent children and broke her sacred marriage covenant with the Lord, her own blood must be shed. The judgment will fall with the fierce, righteous passion of an injured husband.

God will deliver Jerusalem into the hands of the very foreign nations she courted. These conquerors will tear down her pagan altars, strip her of her fine clothes, and loot all her royal jewels. She will be left completely bare and destitute, just like the helpless infant God originally rescued.

The invading armies will act like a legal crowd carrying out a death penalty against a criminal. They will batter down the city's walls with giant siege stones and cut down the people with swords. The punishment physically matches the ancient penalty of stoning for adultery and bloodshed.

The Babylonians will burn Jerusalem's buildings to ashes while the surrounding nations watch the punishment unfold. This terrible ruin will bring a permanent end to the city's idol worship. Having lost all her wealth and freedom, Jerusalem will never again be able to hire foreign lovers.

God's fierce wrath and jealousy will finally come to rest once the full punishment has been carried out. When divine justice has completely dealt with the nation's sin, His active fury will cease and He will be quiet. The fiery judgment must run its full course before peace can return.

differ.view: God's anger rests because His holy justice has completely consumed the guilty nation, like a fire dying down after its fuel is burnt up.
God becoming quiet describes total abandonment, where the Lord stops rebuking the city and gives her up to her final ruin.
